comparison: Perfect agreement on T2DM macaque physiological characterization (C1-C5). Both evaluations find the evidence convincing and well-supported with appropriate statistical validation. OpenEval provides detailed methodological assessment while peer reviewers emphasize the comprehensive nature and importance of the work.

Complete agreement on microbiome alterations (C6-C12). Both evaluations support the findings with OpenEval noting appropriate statistical methods and peer reviewers explicitly praising the comprehensive gut microbiota comparison as a strength.

Full concordance on functional microbiome characterization (C13-C16). Both find the pathway enrichment and CAZy enzyme profiling convincing. OpenEval provides technical validation details while peer reviewers incorporate this into their overall assessment of the multi-omics approach.

Agreement on metabolomic findings (C17-C23). Both evaluations support the identification of metabolite changes and AhR ligands. OpenEval notes reliance on literature for functional consequences (C23), while peer reviewers find the overall metabolomic evidence convincing as part of the comprehensive analysis.

Concordance on incomplete fatty acid oxidation findings (C24-C28). Both evaluations support the acylcarnitine accumulation evidence. OpenEval specifically notes the slightly less stringent p<0.1 threshold, while peer reviewers accept these findings within the broader lipid metabolism dysfunction narrative.

Full agreement on transcriptomic characterization (C29-C34). Both find the RNA-seq analysis with DESeq2 and functional enrichment convincing. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor while peer reviewers incorporate this into their assessment of the comprehensive multi-omics approach.

Complete concordance on co-expression network analysis (C35-C42). Both evaluations support the WGCNA findings and validation through overlap with DEGs and human T2DM associations. OpenEval provides methodological details while peer reviewers find the integrated evidence convincing.

Strong agreement on plasma fatty acid validation (C43-C48). Both support the targeted metabolomic findings and inverse plasma-fecal PA relationship. OpenEval notes reduced sample size (n=7-8) and peer reviewers explicitly mention plasma fatty acid findings as part of the comprehensive comparison strength. OpenEval includes C49 while peer review addresses it separately.

Agreement on inflammatory activation findings (C50-C53). Both find the selective IL-1β elevation and blood cell changes convincing. OpenEval emphasizes the specific inflammatory profile while peer reviewers incorporate inflammation into the overall disease characterization. OpenEval includes C49 while peer review covers C50-C53.

Concordance on microbe-metabolite correlations (C54-C56). Both evaluations support the correlation analysis linking specific microbes to fatty acid metabolites. OpenEval notes that correlation doesn't establish causation and suggests additional validation, while peer reviewers find this central to understanding microbiota-lipid interactions.

Full agreement on FMT experiment demonstrating causative role (C57-C63). Both evaluations strongly support the experimental design and findings. OpenEval emphasizes the four-group design and synergistic requirement, while peer reviewers explicitly praise the verification in mice as a study strength.

Agreement on histological validation (C64-C66). Both support the pathological findings consistent with prediabetes/T2DM. OpenEval suggests quantitative analysis would strengthen qualitative descriptions, while peer reviewers accept these findings as part of comprehensive verification in the mouse model.

Complete concordance on microbiota-mediated PA absorption mechanism (C67-C75). Both evaluations strongly support this key mechanistic finding linking IL-17A/Cd36 regulation to PA absorption. OpenEval provides detailed methodological assessment while peer reviewers emphasize this substantially advances understanding of microbiota-lipid-host interactions.

Full agreement on microbiota transfer and taxa identification (C76-C84). Both support the successful transfer of microbial signatures and disease phenotype. OpenEval notes modest sample size (n=4) is acceptable, while peer reviewers praise the validation of microbiota transferability and specificity.

Strong concordance on integrative mechanistic model (C85). Both evaluations support the synthesis of multi-omics and experimental findings. OpenEval acknowledges some inferential steps while noting consistency with data, and peer reviewers state the work substantially advances understanding of microbiota-lipid-host interactions.

Agreement on multi-omics summary findings (C86-C93). Both support the integrated characterization. OpenEval covers C86-C91, C121-C122 while peer review addresses C86-C93, showing overlap on the comprehensive T2DM characterization with convincing evidence across omics platforms.

Partial overlap on transcriptomic-metabolomic integration (C92-C93). OpenEval notes causal language is inferential but model is biologically plausible. Peer review includes these claims in broader multi-omics summary (R16) finding evidence convincing, showing agreement despite different grouping.

Agreement on microbiome-PA-inflammation pathway (C94-C98). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN noting the causal chain is largely inferential and lacks direct experimental validation, while peer reviewers find the mechanistic pathway convincing as part of the integrative model. This represents a subtle difference in confidence level.

Concordance on PA-induced insulin resistance mechanisms (C99-C101). Both support the mechanistic pathways linking PA to insulin resistance. OpenEval notes causal relationships are inferred rather than experimentally validated through pathway manipulation, while peer reviewers find the pathway-level interpretations convincing based on transcriptomic data.

Agreement on causal FMT findings summary (C103-C105). Both evaluations support the causative role of microbiota established through experimental design. OpenEval emphasizes the requirement for both FMT and PA diet, while peer reviewers highlight this as the central finding substantially advancing understanding.

Strong agreement on R. gnavus mechanistic effects (C106-C114). Both support the integrated mechanistic model linking mucin degradation to barrier disruption and lipid absorption. OpenEval notes lack of direct mono-colonization validation, while peer reviewers find the integrative mechanistic interpretation convincing with comprehensive evidence.

Concordance on protective bacteria roles (C115-C116). Both support the identification of beneficial bacteria and their collective effects. OpenEval notes cautious language acknowledging inferential nature, while peer reviewers accept these findings as part of comprehensive microbiota characterization with convincing evidence.

Agreement on concluding statements about model utility and findings (C117-C120). Both support the conclusions about the macaque model and microbiota-PA interactions. OpenEval notes C120's 'best model' claim is subjective, while peer reviewers emphasize the work's importance and substantial advancement of understanding.

Partial overlap on experimental outcome summary (C123). OpenEval focuses specifically on C123 summarizing the 120-day FMT experiment outcome, while peer review (R23) covers broader summary including C121-C123, both finding the causal demonstration convincing with comprehensive verification.
